title: Land is found
body: Word returns of a land across open water, unpeopled by anyone resembling the Ròdaich. No record survives of who found it first.

title: The report heard at Cathair dhearg
body: The report of the far land is repeated at Cathair dhearg in the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, by three separate crews from the western harbours, none of whom claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three accounts and notes that they agree on the coast and on nothing else.

title: The Choosing
body: A vote — or something the later chronicles call a vote — decides who will go. Volunteers only. No lots are drawn, no conscription recorded.

title: The roll of the willing
body: At Seann Skell the harbour scribes open a roll for those who mean to go, entered by household rather than by name. The roll is kept on boards in the harbour-house, and a later hand notes that entries were struck out as often as they were added.

title: The queen neither commands nor forbids
body: Queen Beathag declares that the crown will neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back. Her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell within the season.

title: The custodians count the cost
body: The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, reckons which of the households holding the customary right to burn the ore have entered the roll. The custody-book puts it at nearly one household in five, and adds that the reckoning was made twice because the first figure was not believed.

title: The ships are built
body: The island's shipwrights, used to modest coastal craft, build vessels meant to survive open water for the first time in Rodian memory.

title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
body: On the river strand below Seann Skell, the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull ever built on Rodos. The island's craft until then were sewn-plank coasters that never slept out of sight of land.

title: The oaks of Doire fhionn
body: The oak grove that gave Doire fhionn its name is felled for the fleet's keels and carried down to the coast by ox-sled. The grove never regrew, and the village kept a name it no longer had a reason for.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship bound
body: Alasdair Saor takes the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into a single fellowship, binding each apprentice for seven years in the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.

title: The trial hull lost off Inis àrsaidh's harbour
body: The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and sailed out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, to be tried in open water, and founders in a following sea. Eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor changes the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the changed pattern.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean
body: Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and turns its hemp fields over entirely to cordage for the fleet. The town's rope trade outlasts the Sundering by some centuries.

title: The sail-cloth levy
body: Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh is asked for a set length of close-woven cloth for sails, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many households paid does not.

title: The star-lore taught at Cuan ruadh
body: Old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors on the island who had ever kept a course by night, teach the fleet's pilots to hold a heading by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part has not survived.

title: The volunteers name their leaders
body: The households on the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose their own leaders: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein. The custody-book records the choice and nothing of how it was made.

title: The handful for the new hearth
body: The vein-house rules on whether departing custodians may carry the ore. Each ship may take one sealed measure, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. The ruling is the only text in the custody-book addressed to people who were leaving.

title: The west quay lengthened
body: The west quay at Seann Skell is lengthened with dressed stone so that the deep hulls can lie alongside it at low water. Masons are brought from the capital to do the work, and the new stones are the ones the later rite would be held on.

title: The provisioning debate
body: A dispute over how much of the island's stored grain the departing ships may take nearly cancels the whole expedition. It is resolved, unrecorded how, within a season.

title: Àth shean shuts its granaries
body: During the dispute over the fleet's grain, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, Tormod mac Coinnich, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them. The watch is kept until the matter is settled, and Tormod is not recorded as holding office afterward.

title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
body: Once the dispute is settled, grain barges are sent down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital and on by coast to Ros àrsaidh and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts the barges passing and makes the count forty-one.

title: The fleet assembled
body: The fleet lies at Seann Skell complete. The custody-book gives it as nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin corrects this to twenty-one, and no one since has been able to settle which is right.

title: The night of lamps
body: On the last night before the sailing, every house along the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning until morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering recorded as a custom, and the town kept it long after the reason was a story.

title: The Setting-Out
body: The volunteers depart west. The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor; the Ròdaich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.

title: The sunwise turn
body: Before going down the Abhainn naomh to open water the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account of them ends at the foot of the pool.

title: The years counted from the turn
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes adopt it only a generation later.

title: A report reaches Seann Skell
body: A report of the fleet reaches Seann Skell. The custody-book does not say how or by whom it came, only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water and missing its end.

title: Two landfalls
body: What fragmentary report ever returns describes two separate coasts reached, not one — the seed, in this telling, of two later peoples rather than one.

title: Mòrag's line struck
body: Queen Beathag removes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Rodos. The act is entered without comment between a grain ruling and the repair of a bridge.

title: The thinning
body: Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing required fades across the departed's own children. By the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Rodos would recognize.

title: The custodians' second reckoning
body: The vein-house counts again the households that hold the right to the ore. The loss is set down as one hand in five, and beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein itself answers no differently for those who stayed.

title: The Mourning Custom
body: Rodos formalizes a mourning rite for the departed that is not quite grief and not quite celebration — reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.

title: The white sorrow first kept at court
body: Queen Beathag keeps the new mourning for her sister in undyed wool, with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and by the next generation it is kept in every harbour town on the island.

title: Population correction
body: With a portion of the obsidian-bonded population gone, Rodian society reorganizes around a smaller, more concentrated custodian class — the shape every later aristocracy inherits.

title: The seven houses of custody
body: The remaining custodian households are regrouped into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. The division is the first in the record to treat the right to the ore as something inherited by house rather than earned by apprenticeship.

title: Death of Queen Beathag
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Rodos to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.

title: The empty harbor rite
body: A ceremony develops around the specific dock the ships departed from, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can precisely date anymore.

title: The harbour at half trade
body: Seann Skell's harbour-master records his berths at half their former use. The fishing households that had crewed the fleet are simply gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean lay off hands for the first time.

title: The second silence
body: A rumor of a second, smaller crossing — fewer ships, no surviving record of a destination — is neither confirmed nor denied by anything that survives.

title: The watch at Ceann mhòr
body: Fishing families at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, taking turns by household. The watch lapses within a generation, and no sail is recorded.

title: The renaming of the west quay
body: The dock the ships departed from is given a new name specifically so ordinary trade could resume using the old one without the association — an early, quiet act of managed forgetting.

title: Cidhe an Diosail
body: In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.

title: Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
body: In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to appear with no object at all, meaning to have chosen the crossing. Scribes of the next century use it this way without explaining it, which is the surest sign it had become ordinary speech.

title: The first generation to never see the sea empty
body: Children born just after the Setting-Out grow up never having known the harbour with those particular ships in it. For them the departure is already history.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor
body: Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.

title: The closing of the shipwrights' guild
body: With no more ocean-crossing vessels needed, the guild that built the Sundering fleet quietly dissolves — its techniques half-forgotten by the time anyone thinks to need them again.

title: The keel-moulds burned
body: The patterns and moulds of the dissolved fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are broken up and burned as firewood during a hard season. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed, not of what was in it.

title: The mountain divided among the houses
body: The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms the Small-Burning measure for each of them. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.

title: The coppice law of Doire fhionn
body: With the great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.

title: The lamps kept at Seann Skell
body: The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, which the priests do not correct.

title: Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is a list of the ore burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first.

title: Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
body: King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and uneventful reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.

title: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
body: The silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is worked into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heir to Sliochd Fhearchair, closes its methods within four families.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet
body: Inis mhòr in the north builds a fleet of barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag and, from Ros chiar at the river mouth, west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none sleeps out of sight of land.

title: The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
body: A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared-meal custom is kept throughout, and the town's reeve credits it with the survival of the rest.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
body: The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings and is rebuilt in stone by its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim. The account of her rebuilding mentions the jugged buffalo it was already known for.

title: The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
body: The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, where the names of the dead of the eastern shires are cut on wooden posts. The posts are recut every generation as the old ones rot.

title: Ìomhar dies without an heir
body: King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and the line of Beathag ends with him. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a successor.

title: Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
body: The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. It is the first crowning in the record decided by the custodian houses rather than by descent.

title: A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: King Fearchar keeps his court for part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, so that the vein-house may be consulted without a journey. The custom of the double court lasts as long as his house.

title: The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
body: The fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich form a single fellowship to share boats and nets after a season of losses. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.

title: Fearchar Donn crowned
body: Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.

title: Gormshuil of the Hawk
body: At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, who is as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, the oldest of men, and remembers everything with him, and that the vein is the Hungry Hawk, who must be fed the measured handful and no more, since a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.

title: The hawk-house at Ros gheal
body: A second house of the Hawk is founded at Ros gheal by Gormshuil's pupils. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for the whole country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.

title: Flood at Seann Vell
body: The river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks in a wet spring and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights rebuild them on the higher bank.

title: The sayings of Gormshuil written
body: After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written down at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and there are more of these than of the rest.

title: The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
body: A northern storm, named in the harbour rolls Am Fuath Mòr, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers are drowned.

title: Seann Toll walls its harbour again
body: Seann Toll rebuilds its harbour wall higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every later storm in this age.

title: The walls of Dùn dhearg
body: Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills is walled in stone by Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land around it. The walls are the first on the island built by a custodian house rather than the crown.

title: Queen Sìleas's measures
body: Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes a single measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Standard firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.

title: Tally-houses in the royal granaries
body: Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first island-wide account of trade, and it runs entirely without coin.

title: The market charter of Cathair fhada
body: Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market each week on its ridge and a tally-house for the south, the first market right cut on paired sticks. The long city's merchants carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and they begin to go to the harvest fair at Muileann òg as one company.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
body: The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened so that two carts can pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, where it can still be read.

title: The crossing days of the panthers
body: Herders in the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar begin keeping the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, driving their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, is recorded as serving oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water, to the ore-carters. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.

title: The house of disputation at Dùn thais
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais where the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.

title: Coinneach's question
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks in open disputation whether the hands that went with the fleet were the ones the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables, which the record notes is the first time they forbade a question rather than an act.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr grows
body: Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms after a run of poor seasons and doubles in size within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.

title: Death of Queen Sìleas
body: Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than half a century. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.

title: The deep hull that would not float true
body: A merchant of Inis àrsaidh pays to have a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run to the east. The wrights cannot remember how Alasdair Saor's keels were scarfed, and the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.

title: Salt pans at Ros fhionn
body: The river town of Ros fhionn in the north-east lays out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats and begins to send salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of value in the north-eastern shires.

title: The wool of Baile gharbh
body: The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. It is also the cloth in which the white sorrow is kept.

title: Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: Traffic over Drochaid Ros fhionn grows so heavy with salt carts that the bridge-keeper is given the right to take a handful from each load. The keeper's salt-box is recorded as holding more than some villages' granaries.

title: The wells crack at Cill ghlas
body: An earth tremor in the hills around Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it and note also that the galleries were untouched.

title: The Hollow Man spoken of again
body: Shepherds of the Doire uaine hills refuse to light fires on the high pastures, citing the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.

title: Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
body: Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is recorded as the first king to learn his letters as a child.

title: Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
body: Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. The mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season from this time on.

title: Clach first preached at Inis thais
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone Clach stands, preaches that the stone is Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out under the rightful king, and that its sworn guards are the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone.

title: The wolf-house at Inis thais
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein's followers raise a temple at Inis thais, the first temple on the island raised to Lia Fàil by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.

title: Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
body: Priests of the Hawk and the Fianna of the Stone both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the arrangement holds.

title: The market inside the new gate
body: Seann Skell on the Hawk bay is walled, and a market is chartered inside the new landward gate. Amber, whale-oil, honey and the sheep of the northern moors are sold there, and the amber-workers of the bay agree to sell no rough amber outside the walls.

title: Macha at court
body: King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha, the grey, and Dubh Sainglenn, the black: two horses, one yoke; light and dark are two powers in balance, and the vein belongs to both. The court follows him, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, becomes the order of Cathair dhearg and the crown.

title: Fire at Tobar dhearg
body: A fire in the thatch spreads through Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. The villagers rebuild with slate from the quarries nearby, and the village is known for its slate roofs after.

title: Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: The share of custody over Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, divided since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha. The other claimants withdraw from the wood without contest, and the record does not say why.

title: The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: The druids of the schools take formal keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the wood of Flidais's white stag, walking its bounds each year. The walk becomes the schools' one public observance.

title: The drovers of Àth chiar
body: Drovers from Àth chiar begin driving cattle over the eastern hills to the mining towns each year. Their routes are the first on the island to be marked with cairns.

title: Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
body: At Doire chiar, Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, revives the teaching of the Holy Age's rival school, that the vein answers effort and not birth, and writes it out in tracts copied by her pupils. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.

title: The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
body: The vein-house orders every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned. Some hundred copies are surrendered. Eilidh herself is not punished and dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.

title: Death of King Aonghas
body: King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of Macha, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.

title: Tormod Bàn crowned
body: Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.

title: Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the central mining road, becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds a second byre for them and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.

title: The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
body: A family at Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Rodos hung in a hawk-house. The bell cracks in its first frost, and the second holds.

title: An Gàire Dubh
body: A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and ruins the season's salt fish. The town is rebuilt a street further back from the shore.

title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
body: Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, its bell rung at each measured burning. The Hawk's teaching holds there when it fades elsewhere in the south.

title: The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
body: Both sons of King Tormod Bàn are drowned when a ferry overturns crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.

title: Death of Tormod Bàn
body: King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir. Three claims are laid before the houses at once.

title: The three claimants
body: The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among them and the War of the Three Claimants begins.

title: Seann Warr shuts its gates
body: Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, closes its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. It is besieged twice in the war and taken by neither.

title: The ford at Àth shean
body: Dùghall Garbh's host meets Raghnall Ruadh's at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.

title: The burning of Doire mhin
body: Raghnall Ruadh's retreating men burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary to deny it to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests.

title: The siege of Cathair dhomhain
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days when its wells are poisoned by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.

title: The hearths refused
body: Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refuses the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths that had been lit with the ore for generations go cold, and the act turns more people against him than any battle.

title: The battle of Muileann chrom
body: The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall is killed on the field and the vein-house is opened by his own custodians the next day.

title: Death of Dùghall Garbh
body: Dùghall Garbh dies of his wounds from Muileann chrom at Baile Mòr dhomhain. His followers go over to Catrìona without a further fight.

title: Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg and is known after as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The War of the Three Claimants ends with her crowning, having lasted about a decade.

title: The ruling of the hearth
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house fix in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves.

title: Catrìona's road south
body: Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone, so that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. The road is known as Rathad na Banrighinn.

title: Seann Warr's gates honoured
body: Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and levy its own tolls, in memory of its standing aside in the war. The grant is cut over the landward gate.

title: Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in one day, which the record remarks on.

title: The Book of the Three Claimants
body: A clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, Seònaid nic Coinnich, writes an account of the war from the custody-book and from the testimony of those who fought. It is the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as a single narrative rather than as entries.

title: The sickness at Inis chrom
body: A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Fianna of the Stone nurse the sick and many of them die of it, and the town becomes the Stone's for good.

title: The oyster beds of Doire shean
body: Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes the village rich enough to be a shire seat.

title: The feast-market at Seann Tarr
body: The crowds that come to the ancestor shrine at Seann Tarr for the great feasts begin to hold a market on the three feast days. Its chief goods are honey, beeswax for the shrine lights and the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich. The wax lights of Seann Tarr are soon burned at ancestor shrines along the whole north-eastern coast.

title: Manannan preached at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power as Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth bears the yellow scorpion, and teaches that Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Rodos from every ship beyond it, and that it must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan.

title: Death of Lachlann mac Iain
body: Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The record calls his reign quiet and means it as praise.

title: Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
body: The teaching of Manannan's order spreads down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean, carried by fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first converts.

title: Within sight of land
body: Manannan's priests at Ros bheag lay it down that no boat of the faithful may go beyond sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and the steering of boats by the stars, already half lost, is lost there entirely.

title: The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
body: The royal granaries at Àth shean, old since before the Sundering, are pulled down and rebuilt in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.

title: The rope-walks shortened
body: Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and puts the ground to barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of that length.

title: Wave at Cnoc chaol
body: A great swell, with no storm behind it, runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village moves its racks further up the shore.

title: The market of the eastern road
body: Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the eastern straight road, is given a market for the east coast. The fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns meet the furs, hides and dyes of the hills there, and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh sell their colours nowhere else.

title: The two counts reconciled
body: The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The day of the empty-harbour rite, which each count had placed differently, is fixed by the same agreement, and later scribes stop pretending it was fixed by evidence.

title: The druid school at Inis mhòr
body: A house of disputation is founded at Inis mhòr by pupils of Dùn thais, and the question of the vein is argued in the north for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.

title: Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
body: Eilidh Bhàn, the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The record of her long reign is almost entirely one of harvests.

title: The bath-house at the hot springs
body: Clann Choinnich rebuilds the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in dressed stone and admits the sick of any house on one day in seven. The house's physicians keep a book of cures that is later lost.

title: The sea-thieves of the north-west
body: Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin taking fish and grain from coasting traders. The sea-thieves are Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names.

title: Baile chrom half empty
body: The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the town's houses empty, their families gone east after the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.

title: The raid on Eilean dhubh
body: A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

title: The dearth on the north-west shore
body: A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore brings a dearth that the shared-meal custom cannot carry. Families leave the coast for the interior and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time until the end of the age.

title: The king-list recopied
body: The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn recopy the king-list of Rodos from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins its account of the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.

title: The strand-market at Àth fhionn
body: Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast. Fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley are sold there, and the fishers of the north coast stop carrying their catch to Inis mhòr.

title: Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
body: Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg with no child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house rather than at the capital.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
body: The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house as well as the crown.

title: The crown and the custody joined
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write it into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. From this time the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodian class and the court are one body.

title: The custody's seal on the king's letters
body: From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters are sealed with the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, with a hollow lozenge over it for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing else. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.

title: Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first ruler to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.

title: The schism of the Hawk
body: A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed forever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a larger flock may be fed a larger handful are called the Fed Hawk.

title: The harbour of Seann Chwen
body: The port of Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole, and becomes the port for the ore-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.

title: The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
body: The priests of the Fed Hawk, turned out of Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. Their teaching is written in the custody-book as an error, and the error is recorded at length.

title: The Fed Hawk's petition
body: The Fed Hawk petitions the king's council from Seann Skell to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. The petition is the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law.

title: The gallery at Cill ghlas
body: A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen custodians' labourers. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names.

title: The ore-roads kept by the crown
body: The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the keeping of the crown, so that the carts carrying the measured ore to the temples may not be stopped by any house. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.

title: The crown's riders
body: Fresh horses are kept for the crown's riders at the waypoint houses on the ore-roads. A rider who changes horses at every house can carry the council's word from Cathair dhearg to the mountain between dawn and dark. The houses are paid for the stabling out of the ore-road tolls.

title: The high pastures of Doire uaine abandoned
body: The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. The reason given is the grazing; everyone asked also mentions the Marbh-bheò.

title: The salt fair at Ros fhionn
body: Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve's count is some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the town's height, and the chronicle calls it the richest place in the north-east.

title: Cathair mhòr the largest town
body: Cathair mhòr passes the capital in size, its market drawing trade from the whole south of the island. The capital remains the seat of the crown and the smaller place.

title: The stair at Toll-dubh
body: Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings, long lost, and find a stair cut into the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house have the entrance walled up; the one quarryman who went down is not recorded as saying what he saw.

title: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr
body: Copper-workers at Cathair mhòr begin making cooking pots that are sold on every road on the island. The pots are marked with the maker's sign, and some survive in the ground.

title: Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. He declines to guess who set it so.

title: Ailean's tables of the old ruins
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill completes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, giving their measures, their stone and the lie of each. He concludes that he cannot say whether one people built all three, and his tables are the reason later scholars could not say either.

title: Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned
body: Mòrag Ruadh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler whose household accounts survive whole.

title: The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned
body: The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they record the attempt.

title: Caol shean's fishing year
body: Caol shean, whose boats fish the east coast from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, lands the largest catch in its roll, so large that salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly and the town goes back to salting.

title: The thousandth year
body: The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the ore on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell. Queen Mòrag Ruadh attends. The record says the flame burned the colour of the vein and that the crowd went home without a word.

title: The market above the mill-race
body: The hill-lords of Baile ghorm hold a market at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, for the farms of the south-east. Grain, clay and honey are its common goods. Its rare good is pearls, which the women of the shore take from the mussel beds in the shallows and which are sold in no other market.

title: The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
body: The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the dress of the seven houses on feast days.

title: The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain
body: A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.

title: The cough at Seann Bhral
body: The swallowing cough reaches the port of Seann Bhral. The harbour is closed by the townsfolk themselves, and the shared-meal custom is kept by leaving food at the town's gate.

title: Queen Beathag Fhionn's closing of the roads
body: Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn back travellers. The cough goes no further west.

title: Muileann dhomhain resettled
body: Muileann dhomhain, emptied by the swallowing cough, is resettled by families from the hills around it, who take the empty houses by lot. The town's older families say they never again knew half their neighbours.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired
body: The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are rebuilt at the cost of the Ros fhionn salt-masters. Their names are cut on the keystones.

title: Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn
body: Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, the first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.

title: The Baile ghorm blue fades
body: The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that comes after is the ordinary blue of the rest of the island.

title: The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned
body: The ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal burn in a lightning fire. The keepers recut the names from memory and from the custody-book, and admit in their roll that some are guesses.

title: The silting of Ros fhionn
body: The Abhainn bheag silts up behind a shifting bar below Ros fhionn, and the salt barges can no longer reach the quays. The salt-masters move their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast.

title: Caol gharbh takes the salt
body: Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the Ros fhionn masters' money.

title: The stone on the neck
body: Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them and settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. They meet at the same stone over every quarrel about the strait after, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.

title: Traffic falls on Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: With the salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts stop crossing Drochaid Ros fhionn. The bridge-keeper's office is abolished, and the bridge is little used from this time.

title: The market-court stays at Ros fhionn
body: The salt-masters take their ships to Caol gharbh but leave their market-court on the headland at Ros fhionn, where the weights and the tally-sticks are kept. The farms and forges of the north-eastern hills go on bringing their goods to it, and the town keeps its market after it has lost its harbour.

title: Seòlaid Ros fhionn
body: With the salt of Ros fhionn going by sea, its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and back west into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.

title: The millers of Muileann shean
body: The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new kind of gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. The gearing spreads to the mills of the north within a lifetime.

title: The Sea-Watcher off the north-west
body: Fishers from the thinned north-west coast report the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, close enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.

title: The table of years at Dùn thais
body: A scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, Raghnall mac Chaluim, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live on average a few years longer than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The record notes the finding with unease and without an answer.

title: The table forbidden
body: The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is closed for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.

title: The great gale at Inis mhòr
body: A gale out of the north-east drives the sea up the river at Inis mhòr before the autumn grain fleet has sailed, higher than anyone then living had seen it. Boats are crushed at their moorings and the grain fleet does not sail until the spring.

title: Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
body: Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The keepers of the Old Spirits renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the proper phase of the moon. The guest-house book records pilgrims from every shire.

title: Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill
body: King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons of different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, each of whom has been told he is the heir.

title: The battle of Cnoc naomh
body: The brothers' war opens when Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar retakes it. The houses divide, four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, is named from this battle.

title: The fire at Ceann mhin
body: Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread from Cathair mhòr.

title: The battle of Muileann ghlas
body: Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive, and his captains are allowed to go home.

title: The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and receives the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.

title: Death of Alasdair Bàn
body: Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.

title: White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: Masons from Ceann leathan buy a veined white stone from the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain for the new front of their temple. The quarry is worked from this time on, and its marble goes south by the carriers' road to every town that can pay for it.

title: Iain Ciar's grain law
body: King Iain Ciar orders that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war, having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread. The law is enforced for as long as he lives.

title: The account of the Brothers' War
body: A clerk of King Iain Ciar, Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, writes the account of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn and is the only account that survives, which later readers have found inconvenient.

title: The inns of the mining roads chartered
body: The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, making their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.

title: Death of Iain Ciar
body: King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years of his death, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef
body: An Taigh-seinnse Òir, on the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first recorded dish of that house; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the bare northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves inside. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint to the charter-roll is recorded in full.

title: The hull that sank at launch
body: Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, sets out to rebuild a deep-keeled hull from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. The hull fills and sinks at its launch, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.

title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east
body: Fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag after their own harbour silts. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.

title: The southern lane
body: The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea and along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had not sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow them. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.

title: The keel-song of Cuan shean
body: A folk-collector of the royal household, Iseabail nic Lachlainn, takes down a work-song still sung by the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it. It is the only record of the Sundering fleet's techniques that survives in any form.

title: The Stone's schism at Inis thais
body: The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say not keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.

title: The grey storm at Seann Tarr
body: A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes in from the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt, but the harbour is not, and its boats move to Cuan ruadh.

title: The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
body: The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.

title: Cuan ruadh's new harbour
body: Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm to take the boats from Seann Tarr. The town prospers on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.

title: Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
body: Catrìona Bheag, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. The record notes that she was small, and that no one said so twice.

title: The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
body: The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.

title: The oath of the seven
body: Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth in her presence, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.

title: Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr
body: The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Rodos in this age. Its black and white floor took eleven years to lay.

title: The eastern Toll-dubh
body: Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tellings, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the two entries in the custody-book are cross-referenced by the scribe.

title: The dry years at Achadh shean
body: Three dry seasons in succession empty the wells of the eastern shires around Achadh shean. The shared-meal custom holds, and grain is carted in from the south by the crown.

title: The water-rights of Achadh shean
body: The reeves of Achadh shean divide the use of the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the division on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation and the lots are never redrawn.

title: The firlot of Àth shean
body: The granary of Àth shean discovers its firlot has been worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been for generations. The reeve's accounts are corrected back as far as anyone can reckon.

title: The grey glaze lost
body: The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. Potters of the town try for a generation to match it and fail.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
body: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair drawing drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. The fair becomes yearly and is the largest in the east.

title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
body: Sìleas Òg, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, named for the queen of the firlot. She is the first ruler in the record to have visited every shire seat.

title: Sìleas Òg's census of hands
body: Queen Sìleas Òg orders a new count of every household holding the right to the ore. The count is smaller than any before it, the right having narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.

title: The fire of Ceann mhin
body: A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, this time without a war to blame. The town is rebuilt with stone gable walls between houses by order of its reeve.

title: The silver smelt refused
body: Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the ore beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, on the ground that the ore burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship.

title: The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
body: The smiths of Dùn dhearg, who had made the custodian houses' ceremonial blades since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. Later blades from Dùn dhearg are ordinary.

title: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
body: The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the surrounding land call it an unwise thing to do and continue to bury their own dead elsewhere.

title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned
body: Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only because his reign is the shortest in the king-list.

title: The synod of Manannan's order
body: The priests of Manannan meet at Seann Skell and restate the rule of sight-of-land. They add a prayer, said at the foot of the river pool, asking Manannan to keep the sea shut: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.

title: Queen Mòrag nic Ailein crowned
body: Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Ailein is crowned after him. She reigns for forty years and leaves the king-list its longest run of entries recording nothing but good harvests and the rite.

title: The ferry at Cidhe Beag
body: A ferry family sets up at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, taking passengers and goods down the river by canoe. The family holds the landing for the rest of the age.

title: The dark wine of Àth shean
body: The growers on the slopes above Àth shean press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that keeps a year in the cask. It is sold along the eastern road, and the road-houses serve it as black wine.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
body: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the Holy Age, are laid up for good as the roads improve. The last of them is kept on the strand as a curiosity.

title: Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
body: An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed, and the keepers read it as a warning without being able to agree what of.

title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
body: Beathag nic Thòmais, a mill-owner's widow of Muileann chaol, begins to buy up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from the houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.

title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol
body: A mill at Muileann chaol begins making paper from rags, the first on Rodos. The custody-book is copied onto paper for the first time in this generation.

title: Three copies of the landfall report
body: Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the report of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and in the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.

title: The north-west coast charted
body: The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.

title: The loft at Muileann chaol
body: Beathag nic Thòmais dies and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol, on condition that nothing in it is burned. The town keeps the condition and very little else of her wishes.

title: King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
body: Tormod mac Ruairidh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and for its length.

title: Manannan's harbour prayer
body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell begin saying their prayer to keep the sea shut on the same day as the empty-harbour rite, so that the two are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.

title: Tormod's bridges
body: King Tormod has stone bridges built across the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in compensation.

title: The panther year
body: The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers no herder can remember, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.

title: Caol gharbh loses the salt
body: The salt pans of Caol gharbh fail as the sea rises over them, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took Ros fhionn's trade is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.

title: Storm at Baile ghorm
body: A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.

title: The rite kept by few
body: The empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that no one present could say on which day the fleet had actually sailed.

title: Cuan dhearg flooded again
body: The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.

title: The house at Dùn thais reopened
body: The house of disputation at Dùn thais, closed and reopened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The druids of the schools accept the condition and argue about the vein instead.

title: Death of King Tormod
body: King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.

title: Queen Gormshuil's progress
body: Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid makes a progress round every shire seat on the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks record the grievances of each shire and the queen answers none of them in writing.

title: The second silver petition
body: Clann Choinnich again asks to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with the support of three of the seven houses. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The record gives the name of the member who changed his vote and not his reason.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the eastern road, is recorded in the charter-roll as feeding the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine. The keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is excused her road dues for a year.

title: The last census of hands
body: The vein-house counts the households holding the right to the ore for the last time in this age. They are fewer than at any count before, and larger. The custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.

title: Timber from the west
body: A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith on Rodos recognizes, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers say. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned.

title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out
body: The night of lamps is kept at Seann Skell by fewer and fewer houses, and at last by none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe records that it was she and not the town.

title: The empty-harbour rite, last entry of the age
body: The empty-harbour rite is kept at Seann Skell by eleven people. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing else.

title: The silver petition laid aside
body: Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again, the member who had turned it having died. The petition is left in the vein-house unanswered, and the record of the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

title: The mist thins
body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell record that the mist on the western sea, which has hidden Rodos from every ship beyond it since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it, lies thinner each winter. They say their prayer, A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte, at every tide, and the fishers of the west coast begin to see the line of the open sea beyond the headlands on still mornings.
